title: Introduction to General Examination of the Patient (Head-to-Toe)
path: Introduction to General Examination of the Patient (Head-to-Toe)

headings.title: Purpose and Principles of Physical Examination
headings.content: A physical examination is a systematic data-collection method used by nurses to evaluate a patient's health status. It combines inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation to gather objective baseline information. This process assists in identifying actual or potential health problems, evaluating the effectiveness of nursing interventions, and monitoring changes in clinical conditions over time.

headings.title: Clinical Environment and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Preparing both the environment and the patient minimizes anxiety and ensures accurate assessment findings. The examination room should offer adequate lighting, privacy, and a comfortable ambient temperature. Before touching the patient, explain each step of the procedure, secure informed consent, and encourage the patient to empty their bladder to enhance physical comfort during abdominal and pelvic palpation.

headings.title: Equipment and Standard Precautions
headings.content: Performing a physical examination requires basic diagnostic tools that must be clean and fully functional. Essential items include a stethoscope, sphygmomanometer, penlight, thermometer, and tape measure. Adhering to standard precautions, such as performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact and wearing gloves when touching body fluids or non-intact skin, protects both the nurse and the patient from cross-contamination.

headings.title: General Survey and Initial Observations
headings.content:
The general survey begins the exact moment the nurse first encounters the patient. It forms an overall gestalt impression by observing distinct clinical markers:
- **Apparent state of health**: Assessing whether the patient looks acutely or chronically ill, frail, or robust.
- **Level of consciousness**: Evaluating alertness, orientation to person, place, and time, and responsiveness to stimuli.
- **Signs of distress**: Noting labored breathing, facial grimacing, sweating, or guarding postures.
- **Stature and body habitus**: Observing nutritional status, body symmetry, and posture.

headings.title: Measurement of Vital Signs
headings.content: Vital signs quantify basic bodily functions and serve as critical indicators of physiological stability. These parameters include body temperature, pulse rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Accurate measurement requires proper equipment calibration and strict adherence to standardized techniques, such as selecting the correct blood pressure cuff size to avoid falsely elevated or lowered readings.

headings.title: Systematic Head-to-Toe Physical Assessment Technique
headings.content:
A head-to-toe examination follows a logical sequence to ensure no body region is overlooked while minimizing unnecessary position changes for the patient. The core techniques are applied in a structured order:
1. **Inspection**: Visual scrutiny of shape, color, symmetry, and movement.
2. **Palpation**: Using the hands to feel texture, temperature, moisture, and tenderness.
3. **Percussion**: Tapping body parts to produce sound waves that evaluate underlying tissue density.
4. **Auscultation**: Listening to sounds generated inside the body using a stethoscope, except when assessing the abdomen, where auscultation precedes palpation to avoid altering bowel motility.

headings.title: Documentation and Clinical Reporting
headings.content: Accurate, timely, and objective documentation is the final crucial step of any physical examination. Notes must use precise medical terminology, avoid vague descriptors like "normal" without context, and accurately reflect abnormal findings without personal bias. Clear records ensure continuity of care across multidisciplinary healthcare teams and serve as a legal record of clinical nursing practice.
